Some of that water soaks into the ground and travels slowly through soil and rock; some runs across the surface and gathers into streams. The streams join into rivers, and the rivers carry the water back toward the sea, so that the whole system turns over again and again without a fixed beginning or end.

Along a shoreline, the daily rhythm belongs to the tides. The gravitational pull of the moon, and to a smaller degree the sun, raises a bulge of water that the turning planet passes beneath, so most coasts see the water rise and fall roughly twice a day. The reach of each tide changes through the month: when the sun and the moon line up, their pulls add together and the range grows; when they sit at a right angle, the range shrinks. Wind and the shape of the seabed can lift or lower a tide well beyond what the calendar alone would predict.

Where a river meets the sea, the fresh and salt waters mix in an estuary, a broad and shifting zone that is neither fully one nor the other. The mixing is gentle or vigorous depending on the tide, the river's flow, and the season. Fine sediment carried down by the river tends to settle where the moving water finally slows, building the mud flats and marsh that fringe many quiet shores and that shift their outline year by year.

These wetlands do a great deal of quiet work. They also shelter young fish and shellfish through the early part of life, which is why a healthy marsh tends to sit beside productive water. The same low ground, though, is the first to feel a rising sea, and its margins are among the places where change shows up earliest.

Taken together, the cycle is a study in slow balance: evaporation and rainfall, the daily breath of the tide, the meeting of river and sea, and the long settling of sediment all keep a shoreline in a rough equilibrium that is always being made and unmade. None of it hurries, and none of it stops.
